# Per-Layer MoE Top-K Routing

## Overview

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B uses 256 experts per layer with top-8 routing. Per-layer top-k reduces computation by using fewer experts in layers where quality impact is minimal.

**Architecture note:** Qwen3.6 model uses the `qwen35moe.cpp` graph builder (inherits from `llm_build_qwen35moe`). Both `qwen35moe.cpp` and `qwen36moe.cpp` are patched identically for per-layer support.

## Setup

The code patches are in `/home/jialine/code/llama.cpp` (private fork). Key changes:

1. **`src/llama-hparams.h`**: Added `std::array<uint32_t, LLAMA_MAX_LAYERS> n_expert_used_per_layer = {}`
2. **`src/llama-model.cpp`**: Parses `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` env var in `load_hparams()` (mutable hparams context)
3. **`src/models/qwen36moe.cpp`**, **`qwen35moe.cpp`**, **`qwen3moe.cpp`**: Use `hparams.n_expert_used_per_layer[il]` in `build_layer_ffn` when > 0
4. **`src/llama-graph.cpp`**: Expert aggregation loop uses `std::min(n_expert_used, hparams.n_expert_used)` to avoid out-of-bounds crash

## Usage

```bash
# Format: "start-end:k,start-end:k,..." (0-indexed layers)
# Unspecified layers keep the model's default (usually 8)
export LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="10-29:7,30-39:6"

# Perplexity benchmark
./build/bin/llama-perplexity \
  -m /home/jialine/dir/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ2_XXS.gguf \
  -f /home/jialine/dir/perplexity-test/big2.txt -ngl 0

# Real inference (must disable thinking mode for Qwen3.6 chat template)
./build/bin/llama-cli -m .../model.gguf -ngl 0 \
  -p "your question" -n 128 --temp 0 \
  --reasoning off --no-display-prompt -c 4096 --single-turn
```

**Important:** Qwen3.6 models have a CoT chat template — always use `--reasoning off` with `llama-cli`.

## Full Benchmark Results (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, IQ2_XXS, CPU)

### Perplexity (PPL) — `big2.txt` (~300 lines Chinese, 5120+ tokens)

| Config | Avg exp | PPL | Δ PPL |
|--------|:---:|-----|:---:|
| 8/8/8 (baseline) | 8.0 | **3.19** | — |
| 7/7/7 | 7.0 | **3.25** | **+1.9%** |
| 8/7/6 | 7.0 | 3.29 | +3.1% |
| 8/6/6 | 6.5 | 3.35 | +5.0% |
| 8/7/5 | 6.25 | 3.38 | +6.0% |
| 8/6/5 | 6.25 | 3.43 | +7.5% |
| 8/6/4 | 6.0 | 3.64 | +14.1% |
| 6/5/4 | 5.0 | 3.72 | +16.7% |
| 4/4/4 (uniform) | 4.0 | 3.84 | +20.4% |
| 4/4/3 | 3.75 | 4.44 | +39.2% |
| 8/5/3 | 5.25 | 4.22 | +32.3% |
| 4/3/2 | 2.75 | 7.15 | +124% ❌ |

### Real Inference Speed — 5 multi-turn cases from iic/ms_agent (CPU, ~256 tokens/gen)

| Config | Avg elapsed | Δ Speed |
|--------|:---:|:---:|
| 8/8/8 (baseline) | 15.4s | — |
| 7/7/7 | 14.1s | **-8.1%** |
| 8/7/6 | 14.3s | -7.3% |
| 8/6/5 | 14.3s | -7.0% |
| 8/6/6 | 14.4s | -6.5% |
| 8/7/5 | 14.4s | -6.2% |
| 8/6/4 | 14.5s | -5.7% |
| 8/5/3 | 13.9s | -9.9% |
| 4/4/4 (uniform) | 12.6s | -18.0% |

### Answer Quality

All 6 tested configs (baseline through 4/4/4) produced **equivalent-quality answers** across all 5 diverse test cases (math problem-solving, literary book review, C++ algorithm, jet lag science, and JavaScript code). The only variation was in the creative book-review task where different configs chose different literary works — a stylistic difference, not a quality degradation.

### Long-Text PPL (long8k.txt, 6,843 tokens, ctx=1024)

| Config | Long PPL | Δ |
|--------|-----|:---:|
| 8/8/8 | 2.17 | — |
| 4/4/4 | 2.70 | +24.4% |
| 4/4/3 | 3.01 | +38.6% |

Degradation proportionally consistent with short text — strategy generalizes across context lengths.

### Stability Boundary

**≥4 experts per layer** required for stable generation. Any layer <4 (e.g. 4/3/2: middle=3, deep=2) causes router probability collapse → garbled output.

### Key Findings

- **Sensitivity: deep > shallow > middle** — last 10 layers most PPL-sensitive
- **4/4/4 is the stability floor** — aggressive but correct, 20% PPL loss, 18% speedup
- **7/7/7 is the conservative choice** — 1.9% PPL loss, 8.1% speedup
- **CPU speed gains are modest (~8-18%)** — MoE FFN not dominant CPU bottleneck
- **Recommended: 4/4/4** for production speed, **7/7/7** for quality-first use cases
- **4/4/4 is fastest (-18%) but PPL +20%** — only for speed-critical scenarios
- **Recommended: 7/7/7** — best overall tradeoff. **8/7/6** as close second if you prefer keeping shallow layers at full capacity

## Q4_K_XL Production Data (May 2026)

Q4_K_XL (21GB) on Ryzen 9700X CPU-only, real llama-server deployment:

| Config | Prompt tok/s | Gen tok/s | TTFT | Notes |
|--------|:-----------:|:---------:|:----:|-------|
| top-8 (default) | ~9.5 | ~6.3 | 2.1s | 38s first-token with thinking |
| **6/5/4** | **18.8** | **9.3** | 2.5s | **2.5s first-token** ✅ |

**6/5/4 layout:** `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="0-9:6,10-29:5,30-39:4"` — shallow:6, middle:5, deep:4.

### llama-server Compatibility

`LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` is parsed at model-load level (`src/llama-model.cpp`), so **llama-server inherits it automatically**. No code changes needed for server/tcp deployment:

```bash
LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="0-9:6,10-29:5,30-39:4" \
llama-server -m model.gguf --port 8080 ...
```

### Production Recommendations (CPU-only)

| Tier | Config | tok/s | Use Case |
|------|--------|:-----:|----------|
| Quality | 7/7/7 | ~8 | Accuracy-critical, PPL +1.9% |
| **Balanced** | **6/5/4** | **9.3** | **Production default** |
| Speed | 4/4/4 | ~10 | High throughput, PPL +20% |

**Always use `--reasoning off`** with llama-cli/server for Qwen3.6 models. The CoT chat template adds 38s first-token latency without it.

**Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model architecture note:** This specific model variant uses `qwen35moe.cpp` (maps to `LLM_TYPE_35B_A3B`, 40 layers). Different from Qwen3.6-235B-A22B which uses `qwen3moe.cpp`. Both files need the same per-layer override patch. If only `qwen3moe.cpp` is patched, the 35B-A3B model will silently ignore `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER`.

**mesh-llm speed results (CPU, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, IQ2_XXS):** With 4/4/4: 24 t/s. Without: 16 t/s. **46% speedup.** Tested via `mesh-llm serve --gguf model.gguf` with `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER=0-39:4` in process environment.

Batch benchmark script at `scripts/bench.py` (copy to `/tmp/moe_bench.py`). Saves baseline to `~/dir/perplexity-test/moe-bench/baseline.json` — never re-run baseline.

```bash
python3 /tmp/moe_bench.py baseline   # one-time baseline
python3 /tmp/moe_bench.py perlayer   # compare any config
```

## Hot-Expert Analysis (4/4/4) — NEGATIVE RESULT

**Expert frequency-based sharding is NOT viable for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.**

Under 4/4/4 routing, the router does NOT concentrate expert selection. On 2000 diverse
agent conversation samples (116K tokens from `train.jsonl`, May 17 2026), all 256 experts
are used in every layer with near-uniform distribution:

| Coverage | Experts needed | % of total |
|----------|:---:|:---:|
| 50% (top-128) | 128 | 59.5% |
| 80% | 186 | 72.7% |
| 90% | 218 | 85.2% |
| 95% | 236 | 92.2% |
| 99% | 252 | 98.4% |
| 100% | 256 | 100% |

Coverage is strictly linear with expert count — there are no "hot experts."
Hot/cold ratio is only 1.5× (most-used expert gets 0.58% vs uniform 0.39%).
**4-way moe-split shard** (64 experts physically sliced): PPL=41.79, NOT USABLE.

A earlier 309-sample run on `big2.txt` (homogeneous text) falsely showed concentration
(middle layers needing only 54 experts for 80%). This was a **corpus-size artifact** —
diverse agent data at scale reveals the true uniform distribution.

The `moe-profile` tool (`tools/moe-profile/moe-profile.cpp`) collects per-token,
per-layer expert selection data. It reads actual tensor dimensions (not hardcoded top-8)
and is compatible with `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER`. Analysis script at `scripts/analyze_coverage.py`.

See `references/hot-expert-profiling.md` for the full moe-profile workflow,

## Porting to Other llama.cpp Forks

When porting per-layer top-k to a different llama.cpp base (e.g., mesh-llm's fork at `/home/jialine/code/Mesh-LLM/llama.cpp`), the 5-file diff is identical to the original fork. Key differences to watch:

| File | Change | Fork-Specific Note |
|------|--------|------|
| `llama-hparams.h` | `n_expert_used_per_layer` array | `LLAMA_MAX_LAYERS=512` (same across all forks) |
| `llama-model.cpp` | Env var parse in `load_hparams()` | Insert after `hparams.rope_type = ...;` |
| `llama-model.cpp` | Log in `print_info()` | Insert after `n_expert_used` line |
| `qwen3moe.cpp` | `n_eff_used` in `build_layer_ffn` | **Qwen3.6 uses qwen3moe.cpp in mesh-llm** (NOT qwen35moe.cpp) |
| `qwen35moe.cpp` | Same override in for-loop | Only needed for Qwen3.5 models; skip for Qwen3.6 |
| `llama-graph.cpp` | `n_agg = min(...)` | **CRITICAL** — without this, OOB crash when per-layer < 8 |

**Verification:** The `load_hparams()` function may be called multiple times during model loading (once per GGUF file opened, once after full model init). Add a `fprintf(stderr, "DEBUG: LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER = '%s'\\n", env ? env : "(null)");` to confirm env var is read. If `n_expert_used_per_layer` fills correctly but the `print_info()` log doesn't appear, the env var IS working — the log system may not be initialized yet at info-print time.

**Build:** mesh-llm's fork uses `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON` then `make -j$(nproc) -C build llama-cli`.

For full integration with mesh-llm's Rust control plane, see `mesh-llm-moe-integration` skill.
200-sample vs 2000-sample comparison data, and analysis methodology.

## Pitfalls

- `moe-profile` must be compiled from the patched source that reads actual tensor dims
  for top-k (not hardcoded 8). Without this fix, per-layer data is incorrect.
- Env var parsed at model load time (`load_hparams`), NOT runtime. Must set before loading.
- **`LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` works with llama-server** — env var is parsed in `llama-model.cpp` which all tools link. No server-specific code needed.
- **`LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` works in mesh-llm** (fixed May 17) — previously only worked with `llama-cli`; root cause was `qwen35moe.cpp` using global `n_expert_used` instead of per-layer `n_expert_used_per_layer[il]`. After patching `qwen35moe.cpp` (same pattern as `qwen3moe.cpp`), mesh-llm's skippy path correctly reads the env var and achieves 46% speedup (24 t/s vs 16 t/s without). The env var is injected via process environment and read by `getenv()` in `llama-model.cpp` — no skippy ABI changes needed.
- **Combined with moe-split**: Per-layer pruning works transparently with moe-split shards — set `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` in each shard's server environment. Each shard independently applies pruning to its own expert set. GPU gains are modest (~5%) vs CPU (~30-50%). See `moe-split` skill for deployment workflow.
- **`llama-graph.cpp` aggregation loop MUST be patched** — original uses `hparams.n_expert_used` for `ggml_view_2d` bounds → OOB crash when per-layer top-k < 8. Fix: `std::min(n_expert_used, hparams.n_expert_used)`.
- Warmup mode uses `n_expert` (256) as top-k — bypasses per-layer settings. Intentional and correct.
- `--reasoning off` required with `llama-cli` (Qwen3.6 CoT template). `--single-turn` needed for non-interactive runs.
- **6/5/4 is the production default** for CPU-only deployments on Q4_K_XL (9.3 tok/s, PPL +17%).
- **Pruning is ineffective on GPU-heavy configs**: When most layers are on GPU (especially -ngl 48 with 0 CPU layers), the bottleneck is GPU memory bandwidth (self-attention weight reads), not FFN expert compute. Top-4 → top-3 saves only ~4ms/token (~5.5%) — within measurement noise. Do not expect speedup from pruning on GPU-centric setups.

## GPU Pruning Results (June 2026)

GPU pruning gains are **much smaller than CPU** because the GPU bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute. FFN expert computation is already fast on GPU.

| Setup | No Pruning | 6/5/4 | Δ |
|-------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| .21 RTX5080 gen | 182 tok/s | 193 tok/s | +6% |
| .21 RTX5080 prompt | 875 tok/s | 955 tok/s | +9% |
| .22 RTX5070Ti gen | 161 tok/s | 169 tok/s | +5% |
| Accuracy (8 tests) | 5/8 | 4/8 | −1 |

**GPU recommendation**: Pruning is optional — 5-9% gain at ~12% accuracy loss. For production GPU deployments, the default top-8 (no pruning) is fine. Only prune if maximizing absolute throughput at the cost of small accuracy loss. For detailed accuracy breakdown (per-shard, per-question), see `moe-split` skill → `references/moe-split-accuracy-benchmark.md`.

## 122B MoE Pruning (48-Layer Layout)

Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (48 layers, 0–47) uses a wider layer layout:

```
Shallow: 0–12 (13 layers) → 6 exp
Middle:  13–37 (25 layers) → 5 exp
Deep:    38–47 (10 layers) → 4 exp
```

Env var: `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="0-12:6,13-37:5,38-47:4"`

3-GPU ggml-rpc TCP distributed results (128 output tokens):

| Config | tok/s | vs 8/8/8 |
|--------|:-----:|:--------:|
| 8/8/8  | 12.7  | — |
| 7/7/7  | 13.0  | +2.4% |
| 6/5/4  | 13.6  | +7.1% |
| 4/4/4  | 14.3  | +12.6% |

Full raw data and methodology in `references/122b-rpc-pruning-results.md`.

## 122B 4-Node RPC Validation (June 21, 2026)

**Status: CONFIRMED EFFECTIVE.** On the 4-node cluster (moe-split `0caeec6b1`, 122B Q4_K_M,
`-sm row -ngl 99`, 256K ctx q8_0 KV, 205-token Chinese prompt), `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="0-47:4"`
produced a **41% speedup** over the default top-8:

| Config | Gen tok/s | Δ |
|--------|:---:|:---:|
| top-8 (default) | 16.61 | — |
| **top-4** | **23.43** | **+41%** |

**Validation method**: A/B test with identical long Chinese prompt (205 tokens prompt,
300 tokens gen), temp=0, measured via `/v1/completions` wall time. Server log confirmed
`print_info: moe topk per layer = 4,4,4,...,4` (48 layers). Model default confirmed via
GGUF metadata: `qwen35moe.expert_used_count = [8]` (256 total experts).

**Contrast with earlier results**: The 3-GPU test (June 9, `-sm layer -ngl 30`, short
English prompt) showed only +12.6% for 4/4/4. The 41% gain here comes from a combination:
full GPU layers (`-ngl 99`), row-split parallelism, and longer prompts that better exercise
FFN compute. **Long prompts (>100 tokens) are better for MoE pruning benchmarks** — short
prompts are dominated by fixed overhead (CUDA graph construction, RPC serialization).

**Benchmarking tip**: Use prompts ≥200 tokens for MoE pruning speed tests. Short prompts
(<50 tokens) understate pruning gains because prompt processing overhead dominates.

## 122B 4-Node -ngl 48: Further Pruning Below 4 — NEGATIVE

While top-8→top-4 yields +41%, **further pruning top-4→top-3 on this setup saved only
~4ms per token** (out of ~72ms total) — ~5.5% theoretical max, zero observable gain
(13.80 vs 13.77 tok/s). The bottleneck shifts from FFN compute to GPU memory bandwidth
during self-attention weight reads once experts are already reduced to 4. **Do not
prune below 4 experts per layer on this hardware.**

**Expert frequency-based sharding is NOT viable for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.**

Under 4/4/4 routing, the router does NOT concentrate expert selection. On 2000 diverse
agent conversation samples (116K tokens from `train.jsonl`, May 17 2026), all 256 experts
are used in every layer with near-uniform distribution:

| 80% | 186 | 72.7% |
| 90% | 218 | 85.2% |
| 95% | 236 | 92.2% |
| 99% | 252 | 98.4% |
| 100% | 256 | 100% |

Coverage is strictly linear with expert count — there are no "hot experts."
Hot/cold ratio is only 1.5× (most-used expert gets 0.58% vs uniform 0.39%).

(middle layers needing only 54 experts for 80%). This was a **corpus-size artifact** —
diverse agent data at scale reveals the true uniform distribution.

## Porting to Other llama.cpp Forks

When porting per-layer top-k to a different llama.cpp base (e.g., mesh-llm's fork at `/home/jialine/code/Mesh-LLM/llama.cpp`), the 5-file diff is identical to the original fork. Key differences to watch:

| File | Change | Fork-Specific Note |
|------|--------|------|
| `llama-hparams.h` | `n_expert_used_per_layer` array | `LLAMA_MAX_LAYERS=512` (same across all forks) |
| `llama-model.cpp` | Env var parse in `load_hparams()` | Insert after `hparams.rope_type = ...;` |
| `llama-model.cpp` | Log in `print_info()` | Insert after `n_expert_used` line |
| `qwen3moe.cpp` | `n_eff_used` in `build_layer_ffn` | **Qwen3.6 uses qwen3moe.cpp in mesh-llm** (NOT qwen35moe.cpp) |
| `qwen35moe.cpp` | Same override in for-loop | Only needed for Qwen3.5 models; skip for Qwen3.6 |
| `llama-graph.cpp` | `n_agg = min(...)` | **CRITICAL** — without this, OOB crash when per-layer < 8 |

**Verification:** The `load_hparams()` function may be called multiple times during model loading (once per GGUF file opened, once after full model init). Add a `fprintf(stderr, "DEBUG: LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER = '%s'\\n", env ? env : "(null)");` to confirm env var is read. If `n_expert_used_per_layer` fills correctly but the `print_info()` log doesn't appear, the env var IS working — the log system may not be initialized yet at info-print time.

**Build:** mesh-llm's fork uses `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON` then `make -j$(nproc) -C build llama-cli`.

For full integration with mesh-llm's Rust control plane, see `mesh-llm-moe-integration` skill.

## Pitfalls

- `moe-profile` must be compiled from the patched source that reads actual tensor dims
  for top-k (not hardcoded 8). Without this fix, per-layer data is incorrect.
- Env var parsed at model load time (`load_hparams`), NOT runtime. Must set before loading.
- **`LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` works with llama-server** — env var is parsed in `llama-model.cpp` which all tools link. No server-specific code needed.
- **`LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` works in mesh-llm** (fixed May 17) — previously only worked with `llama-cli`; root cause was `qwen35moe.cpp` using global `n_expert_used` instead of per-layer `n_expert_used_per_layer[il]`. After patching `qwen35moe.cpp` (same pattern as `qwen3moe.cpp`), mesh-llm's skippy path correctly reads the env var and achieves 46% speedup (24 t/s vs 16 t/s without). The env var is injected via process environment and read by `getenv()` in `llama-model.cpp` — no skippy ABI changes needed.
- **Combined with moe-split**: Per-layer pruning works transparently with moe-split shards — set `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER` in each shard's server environment. Each shard independently applies pruning to its own expert set. GPU gains are modest (~5%) vs CPU (~30-50%). See `moe-split` skill for deployment workflow.
- **`llama-graph.cpp` aggregation loop MUST be patched** — original uses `hparams.n_expert_used` for `ggml_view_2d` bounds → OOB crash when per-layer top-k < 8. Fix: `std::min(n_expert_used, hparams.n_expert_used)`.
- Warmup mode uses `n_expert` (256) as top-k — bypasses per-layer settings. Intentional and correct.
- `--reasoning off` required with `llama-cli` (Qwen3.6 CoT template). `--single-turn` needed for non-interactive runs.
- **6/5/4 is the production default** for CPU-only deployments on Q4_K_XL (9.3 tok/s, PPL +17%).
- **Pruning is ineffective on GPU-heavy configs**: When most layers are on GPU (especially -ngl 48 with 0 CPU layers), the bottleneck is GPU memory bandwidth (self-attention weight reads), not FFN expert compute. Top-4 → top-3 saves only ~4ms/token (~5.5%) — within measurement noise. Do not expect speedup from pruning on GPU-centric setups.

## GPU Pruning Results (June 2026)

GPU pruning gains are **much smaller than CPU** because the GPU bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute. FFN expert computation is already fast on GPU.

| Setup | No Pruning | 6/5/4 | Δ |
|-------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| .21 RTX5080 gen | 182 tok/s | 193 tok/s | +6% |
| .21 RTX5080 prompt | 875 tok/s | 955 tok/s | +9% |
| .22 RTX5070Ti gen | 161 tok/s | 169 tok/s | +5% |
| Accuracy (8 tests) | 5/8 | 4/8 | −1 |

**GPU recommendation**: Pruning is optional — 5-9% gain at ~12% accuracy loss. For production GPU deployments, the default top-8 (no pruning) is fine. Only prune if maximizing absolute throughput at the cost of small accuracy loss. ## 122B 4-Node RPC Validation (June 21, 2026)

**Status: CONFIRMED EFFECTIVE.** On the 4-node cluster (moe-split `0caeec6b1`, 122B Q4_K_M,
`-sm row -ngl 99`, 256K ctx q8_0 KV, 205-token Chinese prompt), `LLAMA_MOE_TOPK_PER_LAYER="0-47:4"`
produced a **41% speedup** over the default top-8:

| Config | Gen tok/s | Δ |
|--------|:---:|:---:|
| top-8 (default) | 16.61 | — |
| **top-4** | **23.43** | **+41%** |

**Validation method**: A/B test with identical long Chinese prompt (205 tokens prompt,
300 tokens gen), temp=0, measured via `/v1/completions` wall time. Server log confirmed
`print_info: moe topk per layer = 4,4,4,...,4` (48 layers). Model default confirmed via
GGUF metadata: `qwen35moe.expert_used_count = [8]` (256 total experts).

**Contrast with earlier results**: The 3-GPU test (June 9, `-sm layer -ngl 30`, short
English prompt) showed only +12.6% for 4/4/4. The 41% gain here comes from a combination:
full GPU layers (`-ngl 99`), row-split parallelism, and longer prompts that better exercise
FFN compute. **Long prompts (>100 tokens) are better for MoE pruning benchmarks** — short
prompts are dominated by fixed overhead (CUDA graph construction, RPC serialization).

**Benchmarking tip**: Use prompts ≥200 tokens for MoE pruning speed tests. Short prompts
(<50 tokens) understate pruning gains because prompt processing overhead dominates.

## 122B 4-Node -ngl 48: Further Pruning Below 4 — NEGATIVE

While top-8→top-4 yields +41%, **further pruning top-4→top-3 on this setup saved only
~4ms per token** (out of ~72ms total) — ~5.5% theoretical max, zero observable gain
(13.80 vs 13.77 tok/s). The bottleneck shifts from FFN compute to GPU memory bandwidth
during self-attention weight reads once experts are already reduced to 4. **Do not
prune below 4 experts per layer on this hardware.**
